question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
One of the students is always / late to the class; he has been warn / by the teacher many times; / but still, he keeps on being late.
option_1: One of the students is always
option_2: but still, he keeps on being late
option_4: late to the class; he has been warn
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. late to the class; he has been warn.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "he has been warn". Since the auxiliary "has been" (Present Perfect Passive) is used, it must be followed by the past participle (V3) form of the verb, not the base form.

• Rule — Present Perfect Passive: Subject + has/have + been + V3.

• The verb "warn" is the base form (V1); its past participle is "warned". The segment should correctly read "he has been warned".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "One of the students is always" is grammatically correct — "One of the + plural noun" correctly takes a singular verb "is".

• Option 2: "but still, he keeps on being late" is correct — "keep on + V-ing" is a standard structure meaning to continue doing something.

• Option 3: "by the teacher many times;" is correct — it properly identifies the agent of the passive action.

NOTE

• "One of the + plural noun + singular verb" is a very frequently tested SSC rule (e.g., "One of the boys is absent").

• Common irregular verb form tested here: warn – warned – warned; many candidates wrongly leave it in the base form after a perfect auxiliary.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully.
The percentage of employees who called in sick and the number of employees who left their jobs within 2 years (were reflective of the level of job satisfaction).
option_1: are reflective of the level of job satisfaction
option_2: is reflective of the level of job satisfaction
option_3: has reflected the level of job satisfaction
option_4: were reflective on the level of job satisfaction
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. are reflective of the level of job satisfaction.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence has a compound subject — "The percentage of employees..." and "the number of employees..." — joined by "and". Two distinct singular subjects joined by "and" together take a plural verb.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: Singular subject + and + singular subject = plural verb (unless the two nouns together refer to a single idea).

• Since both subjects describe two separate statistics being compared, the verb must be plural: "are reflective of". The correct preposition after "reflective" is "of", not "on".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is" is a singular verb, which does not agree with the compound plural subject.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "has reflected" is also a singular verb form (Present Perfect, singular), and it changes the intended meaning to a completed single action rather than a continuing state.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "were" shifts the tense to past unnecessarily, and "reflective on" is an incorrect preposition — the correct usage is "reflective of".

NOTE

• When two singular subjects are joined by "and", use a plural verb, e.g., "Ram and Shyam are here."

• Exception: when the two nouns together refer to a single entity or idea, a singular verb is used, e.g., "Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast."

• Common confusing prepositions: reflective of, indicative of, dependent on, based on.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. Omnivores get energy and nutrients from plant and animal materials by digesting carbs, protein, fat and fibre and metabolising the nutrients and energy of the sources ingested.
B. The many diverse animals categorised as omnivores may be divided into sub-categories based on their dietary habits.
C. An omnivore is an animal that can feed and thrive on both, plant and animal substances.
D. They also have the capacity to integrate food sources like algae, fungus and bacteria into their diet.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. CADB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C is the opening sentence as it introduces and defines the topic — "An omnivore is an animal that can feed and thrive on both, plant and animal substances."

• Sentence A logically follows C, elaborating on HOW omnivores obtain energy — "Omnivores get energy and nutrients from plant and animal materials..."

• Sentence D continues this idea with the connector "They also have the capacity...", adding further food sources omnivores can use.

• Sentence B concludes the paragraph by introducing the broader classification of omnivores into sub-categories, which naturally follows after their feeding habits have been described.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (CADB).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (CABD) is incorrect because placing B (sub-categories) before D (additional diet capacity) breaks the logical flow — D continues directly from A using "also".

• Option 2 (ACDB) is incorrect because starting with A instead of C removes the topic-defining sentence from the beginning, leaving "Omnivores" undefined at the outset.

• Option 4 (DCBA) is incorrect because it starts with "They also have the capacity...", using the pronoun "They" and the word "also" without first establishing what is being referred to.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, look for the sentence that introduces the subject/topic without any pronoun reference — this is usually the opening sentence.

• Words like "also", "however", "therefore", "they", "this" are connector clues — they cannot begin a paragraph as they refer back to something already mentioned.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the following sentence.
Roads in villages during rainy seasons become muddy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. filthy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "muddy" means covered with or full of mud; dirty. (कीचड़ से सना हुआ, गंदा)
◦ Example: After the rain, the field became muddy and difficult to walk on.

• "Filthy" means extremely dirty, which is the closest match in meaning to "muddy" in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Fuzzy" (धुंधला/अस्पष्ट): covered with fine light hair or fluff, or indistinct/blurred — unrelated to dirtiness.

• Option 3: "Blurred" (धुंधला): not clear in outline or shape; smeared — relates to vision/clarity, not dirt.

• Option 4: "Unsoiled" (साफ, बिना गंदगी का): this is an antonym of "muddy", not a synonym, as it means clean and free from dirt.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "muddy": grimy, mucky, slushy, soiled.

• Do not confuse "fuzzy" and "blurred" (both mean unclear/indistinct) with "muddy"/"filthy" (both mean dirty) — they belong to different meaning groups despite superficial similarity in some contexts.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The poet managed to paint a vivid picture of the landscape by the river through words.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Evocative.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "vivid" means producing powerful feelings or clear, sharply defined images in the mind. (स्पष्ट, जीवंत)
◦ Example: She gave a vivid description of her trip to the mountains.

• "Evocative" means bringing strong images, memories, or feelings to mind, which closely matches the sense of "vivid" as used here — the poet's words create a strong mental picture.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Metaphoric" (रूपक संबंधी): relating to the use of metaphor (a figure of speech); not about clarity or vividness of image.

• Option 3: "Contemporary" (समकालीन): belonging to the present time; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "Blurred" (धुंधला): unclear or indistinct — this is actually opposite in meaning to "vivid".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "vivid": graphic, striking, lifelike, vibrant.

• Antonyms of "vivid": dull, faint, vague, blurred.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
I was fascinated by the novel.
option_1: The novel was fascinated to me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The novel fascinated me.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "I was fascinated by the novel" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "the novel" becomes the subject; the verb "fascinated" (V3) becomes "fascinated" (V2, same form since it is a regular verb); and "I" becomes the object "me".
◦ Active: The novel fascinated me.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect as it retains a passive-like structure ("was fascinated to me") which is neither correct active nor correct passive voice.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "fascinate" is the base form (V1); the sentence needs the past form "fascinated" (V2) to match the tense of the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "fascinates" is in the Simple Present Tense, which changes the tense of the original Simple Past sentence.

NOTE

• When converting passive to active voice, always preserve the original tense of the sentence.

• Regular verbs like "fascinate" have identical V2 and V3 forms ("fascinated"), which often causes confusion — check the tense of the sentence carefully to select the correct form.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
There lies no guarantee that the hierchical structural framework between the elite and downtrodden sections of the society is right.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. hierchical.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "hierarchical" — relating to a system in which people or things are ranked one above another according to status or authority.
◦ Example: The company follows a strict hierarchical structure of management.

• Spelling key: HIER + ARCH + ICAL. The word "hierchical" as printed in the sentence is missing the syllable "ar" — it should read hier-ar-chical, not hier-chical.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "guarantee" is spelt correctly — a formal promise or assurance.

• Option 3: "structural" is spelt correctly — relating to the structure or framework of something.

• Option 4: "downtrodden" is spelt correctly — oppressed or treated badly by people in power.

NOTE

• The related noun is hierarchy, and the adverb is hierarchically.

• Other commonly misspelt words with tricky letter combinations at SSC level: bureaucracy, questionnaire, embarrass, occurrence, hierarchy.

question: Select the sentences that contains no spelling errors.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Diabetes is a chronic disease.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Diabetes" — a medical condition in which the body cannot properly control the amount of sugar in the blood.
◦ Example: Diabetes is a chronic disease that requires careful management of diet and lifestyle.

• Spelling key: DIA + BE + TES. Note the sequence "be" before "tes" — there is no extra "i" after "d" and no letters interchanged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Diabeties" — incorrect; an extra "i" has been wrongly inserted before "es".

• Option 3: "Daibetes" — incorrect; the letters "a" and "i" after "D" have been interchanged.

• Option 4: "Diabites" — incorrect; "be" has been wrongly replaced with "bi".

NOTE

• The related adjective is diabetic.

• Other commonly misspelt medical/scientific terms at SSC level: pneumonia, rheumatism, haemorrhage, questionnaire, cemetery.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The man who / was committed / the theft last night / was caught this evening.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. was committed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "was committed". The verb "commit" must be used in the active voice, simple past tense here, since "the man" is the one performing the action of committing the theft, not receiving it.

• Rule: When the subject itself performs the action described by the verb, the verb should be in the active voice (Subject + V2 + Object), not the passive voice (Subject + was/were + V3).

• The segment should correctly read "committed" (active, simple past) instead of "was committed" (passive).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "was caught this evening." is correct — here passive voice is appropriate since "the man" is the receiver of the action of catching.

• Option 3: "The man who" is grammatically correct as a relative clause opener.

• Option 4: "the theft last night" is correct — it is simply the object of the verb "committed" along with a time adverbial.

NOTE

• Do not confuse two verbs within the same sentence — here "caught" is rightly passive (the man was caught by someone) while "committed" must be active (the man committed the theft himself).

• Common SSC trap: mixing active and passive constructions within a single complex sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Health club membership has grown by leaps and bounds after the pandemic.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. very quickly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "by leaps and bounds" means very quickly and in large amounts; with rapid progress. (बहुत तेज़ी से)
◦ Example: Her English has improved by leaps and bounds since she joined the coaching class.

• The idiom is used to describe growth or progress that happens rapidly and dramatically, which matches the context of "health club membership has grown... after the pandemic."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "slowly and gradually" is incorrect — it is nearly opposite in meaning to the idiom, which denotes speed, not gradual change.

• Option 2: "full of speed and excitement" is incorrect — while it references speed, it wrongly adds a sense of excitement/thrill that the idiom does not carry; the idiom simply denotes rapid growth or increase.

• Option 3: "hurriedly" is incorrect — "hurriedly" suggests a rushed, possibly careless manner, whereas "by leaps and bounds" simply denotes fast, substantial progress or growth.

NOTE

• Other idioms of speed often asked in SSC: "in a jiffy" (very quickly), "at the drop of a hat" (immediately), "like a house on fire" (very fast/well, especially of a relationship or activity).

• "Leaps and bounds" literally refers to jumping motions, used figuratively for rapid advancement.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Steer clear of
option_1: Show someone how to do a job or activity
option_3: Avoid someone or something because it is dangerous for you
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Avoid someone or something because it is dangerous for you.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Steer clear of" means to deliberately avoid someone or something, especially because it is risky, unpleasant, or dangerous. (किसी चीज़ से दूर रहना/बचना)
◦ Example: You should steer clear of junk food if you want to stay healthy.

• The idiom comes from the literal act of steering a vehicle or vessel away from an obstacle to avoid collision, used figuratively to mean avoiding trouble.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Show someone how to do a job or activity" (काम करना सिखाना): this is closer to the meaning of the idiom "show someone the ropes".

• Option 2: "Be very easy" (बहुत आसान होना): this matches idioms like "a piece of cake" or "child's play", not "steer clear of".

• Option 4: "Be mentally and physically exhausted" (थका हुआ होना): this matches idioms like "burnt out" or "dead beat", not "steer clear of".

NOTE

• Related idioms of avoidance: "give a wide berth to" (to avoid), "keep at arm's length" (to avoid getting too close to someone).

• "Steer clear of" is commonly followed by a noun/gerund, e.g., "steer clear of arguments".

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
The students decided to surprise their teacher on her birthday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No substitution.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "their teacher on her birthday" is already grammatically correct as it stands.

• "Their" correctly refers back to the plural subject "The students" (a common teacher shared by many students), "her birthday" correctly refers to the teacher (singular, female), and "on" is the correct preposition to use with a specific day/occasion like a birthday.

• Since no grammatical or usage error exists in the original segment, it should be left unchanged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "their teacher at her birthday" is incorrect — the preposition "at" is not correctly used with "birthday"; the correct preposition is "on" (used with specific calendar days/dates/occasions).

• Option 2: "there teacher on her birthday" is incorrect — "there" (an adverb of place) is wrongly used instead of the possessive pronoun "their".

• Option 3: "her teacher on her birthday" is incorrect — replacing "their" with "her" wrongly implies only one student has this teacher, and also creates ambiguity as to whose birthday "her" refers to.

NOTE

• Preposition rule: use "on" with specific days and dates (on Monday, on 5th May, on his birthday); use "at" with specific points in time (at noon, at midnight).

• Do not confuse the homophones "there" (place), "their" (possessive), "they're" (they are) — a very common SSC error-spotting trap.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The driver was taken to the nearest dispensary by the beggars.
option_1: The beggars take the driver to the nearest dispensary.
option_2: The beggars took the driver to dispensary.
option_3: The beggars took the driver to the nearest dispensary.
option_4: To the nearest dispensary, the beggars took the driver.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The beggars took the driver to the nearest dispensary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The driver was taken to the nearest dispensary by the beggars" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "the beggars" becomes the subject; "was taken" (V3) becomes "took" (V2); and "the driver" becomes the object, with the complete phrase "to the nearest dispensary" retained unchanged.
◦ Active: The beggars took the driver to the nearest dispensary.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "take" (present tense) does not match the Simple Past Tense of the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it drops the word "nearest", changing the meaning/content of the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because, although it conveys the same idea, it unnecessarily inverts the natural subject-verb-object word order of a standard active sentence, which is not the conventional way to express active voice in such conversions.

NOTE

• While converting voice, all details of the original sentence (adjectives like "nearest", adverbials, etc.) must be retained exactly.

• Ensure the tense of the converted sentence exactly matches the tense of the original sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
He was sitting besides his best friend during the event.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. was sitting beside his.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The words "beside" and "besides" are commonly confused. "Beside" is a preposition meaning next to, while "besides" means in addition to or apart from.

• Since the sentence describes physical proximity ("He" sitting next to his best friend), the correct preposition is "beside", not "besides".

• The subject "He" is singular and matches the singular verb "was", and "his" correctly agrees with the subject "He" (masculine, possessive).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "was sitting about his" is incorrect — "about" means "concerning" or "approximately", which does not fit the context of physical location.

• Option 3: "were sitting besides his" is incorrect — "were" does not agree with the singular subject "He" (should be "was"), and "besides" is still the wrong word.

• Option 4: "was sitting besides her" is incorrect — "besides" remains wrong, and "her" incorrectly changes the gender of the possessive pronoun, which should match "He" i.e. "his".

NOTE

• Beside = next to (position); Besides = in addition to / apart from (used to add information).
◦ Example: Besides being a good singer, she is also an excellent dancer. (in addition to)

• Other commonly confused word pairs at SSC level: "beside/besides", "farther/further", "later/latter", "among/between".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The efforts of the doctors came to a futile end with the death of the patient.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Fruitless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "futile" means producing no useful result; pointless or unsuccessful. (व्यर्थ, निष्फल)
◦ Example: All his attempts to fix the old car proved futile.

• "Fruitless" carries the same sense of yielding no positive result or success, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Enriching" (समृद्ध करने वाला): making something better in quality; the opposite sense of "futile".

• Option 3: "Startling" (चौंकाने वाला): causing sudden shock or surprise; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "Terrifying" (भयानक): causing extreme fear; unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "futile": useless, vain, ineffective, unproductive.

• Antonyms of "futile": fruitful, effective, successful, productive.

question:
Complete the following collocation.
When I got the job, I knew what _______ money really is.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. hard-earned.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hard-earned" is a fixed collocation meaning obtained through great effort or hard work, and it is conventionally used with the noun "money".
◦ Example: He spent his hard-earned money on his sister's education.

• Collocations are fixed combinations of words that native speakers habitually use together; other combinations, even if logically plausible, are not standard usage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "effort-earned" is incorrect — this is not a recognised or standard English collocation.

• Option 2: "soft-earned" is incorrect — this combination is not used in English; it is not a recognised collocation.

• Option 4: "honest-earned" is incorrect — the standard way to describe money obtained honestly is "honestly earned" (adverb + past participle), not "honest-earned" (adjective + past participle) as a compound.

NOTE

• Other common "hard-" collocations: hard-working, hard-hitting, hard-pressed, hardcore.

• Collocation questions must be learnt as fixed word combinations rather than derived through logic alone, since SSC frequently tests such fixed usages.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Russell Wilson, an NFL
P. about Naomi Osaka saying that her
Q. has been spectacular to watch
R. humility and dedication to others
S. player for the Seattle Seahawks, wrote
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. SPRQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with "Russell Wilson, an NFL", which must be completed by identifying his profession before the main verb — this is done by S: "player for the Seattle Seahawks, wrote".

• This is followed by P: "about Naomi Osaka saying that her", introducing the subject of what he wrote about.

• Next comes R: "humility and dedication to others", the qualities of Naomi Osaka being described (grammatically completing "her humility and dedication to others").

• Finally, Q: "has been spectacular to watch" completes the sentence as the verb phrase describing these qualities.

• Full sentence: "Russell Wilson, an NFL player for the Seattle Seahawks, wrote about Naomi Osaka saying that her humility and dedication to others has been spectacular to watch."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (SPRQ).

Additional Information

• Option 2 (PRQS) is incorrect because it places "about Naomi Osaka..." directly after "an NFL", which is grammatically incomplete and meaningless without first stating Wilson's profession (S).

• Option 3 (RPQS) is incorrect because it begins with "humility and dedication to others", which has no grammatical subject or reference at that point in the sentence.

• Option 4 (QPRS) is incorrect because it begins with "has been spectacular to watch", which cannot logically or grammatically follow "an NFL".

NOTE

• In para/sentence jumble questions, first identify the part that grammatically completes the given opening fragment before looking for logical/thematic connections among the rest.

• Look out for pronouns like "her" and "that" as connective clues linking two segments together.

question:
Select the most appropriate collocating word to fill in the blank.
This statement of the political leader has created________confusion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. utter.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Utter confusion" is a fixed collocation meaning complete or total confusion, and "utter" is the standard intensifying adjective used with "confusion" in English.
◦ Example: The sudden announcement caused utter confusion among the employees.

• Collocations must be memorised as fixed word pairings, since other adjectives with similar meanings may not be conventionally paired with the same noun.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "heavy" is incorrect — "heavy" collocates with words like "heavy rain", "heavy traffic", "heavy loss", but not conventionally with "confusion".

• Option 3: "weighty" is incorrect — "weighty" collocates with words like "weighty matter" or "weighty issue", not with "confusion".

• Option 4: "vast" is incorrect — "vast" collocates with words like "vast area", "vast experience", "vast majority", but not conventionally with "confusion".

NOTE

• Other common "utter" collocations: utter nonsense, utter disregard, utter chaos, utter disbelief.

• Collocation-based questions are best prepared by reading extensively and noting down frequently paired words, since they cannot always be derived logically.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
Marcella seemed morose and downcast when she refused to have dinner.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gloomy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "morose" means sullen and ill-tempered; gloomy and unhappy. (उदास, चिड़चिड़ा)
◦ Example: He has been morose ever since he lost his job.

• "Gloomy" carries the same sense of sad and depressed, matching the tone already set by "downcast" in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Jocund" (प्रसन्नचित्त): cheerful and lighthearted — this is actually an antonym of "morose".

• Option 2: "Excited" (उत्साहित): feeling great enthusiasm; unrelated and opposite in tone to the sentence's context.

• Option 4: "Liberal" (उदार): open to new ideas, generous; unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "morose": sullen, sulky, glum, dour, melancholy.

• Antonyms of "morose": cheerful, jovial, jocund, buoyant.

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
Shravan said that the prisoner had slept throughout the journey.
option_1: Shravan said, "The prisoner sleeps throughout the journey."
option_2: Shravan said, "The prisoner had been sleeping throughout the journey."
option_3: Shravan says, "The prisoner has slept throughout the journey."
option_4: Shravan said, "The prisoner had slept throughout the journey."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Shravan said, "The prisoner had slept throughout the journey."

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given indirect (reported) sentence uses the reporting verb "said" (past tense) and the reported verb "had slept" (Past Perfect Tense).

• Rule — Narration: When the tense of the reported speech is already Past Perfect, it remains unchanged while converting to direct speech, because Past Perfect is the "back-shifted" form of the Simple Past/Present Perfect and there is no further tense to shift it to.

• Since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, the reporting verb in direct speech also remains "said", and the tense inside the quotation marks stays exactly as "had slept".
◦ Direct: Shravan said, "The prisoner had slept throughout the journey."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "sleeps" (Simple Present) does not correctly reverse the Past Perfect tense used in the indirect speech.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "had been sleeping" is Past Perfect Continuous, which changes the aspect of the original verb "had slept" (Past Perfect simple, not continuous).

• Option 3 is incorrect because it changes the reporting verb to "says" (present tense) and the reported verb to "has slept" (Present Perfect), both of which are inconsistent with the past reporting verb "said" used in the indirect sentence.

NOTE

• The Past Perfect Tense (had + V3) does not change when converted between direct and indirect speech, in either direction — it is the tense that other past tenses shift INTO, not out of.

• Always match the reporting verb tense in the direct form to the reporting verb tense given in the indirect sentence.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Comics have (1) _________ many superheroes. Bantul, the great was (2) _________ in the year 1965 in the backdrop of the Indo-Pak war. Indrajal comics was set up in 1964 and (3) __________ Aabid Surti, who gave birth to a character called Bhadur in 1976 wearing kurta and jeans. Raj comics too (4) _________ into this sphere with their (5) _________ toons Nagraj, Tiranga and Shakti together called Brahman Rakshak (protectors of the universe).

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. produced.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb that naturally collocates with "superheroes" in the context of comics creating fictional characters. "Produced" fits naturally, meaning comics have given rise to many superheroes.

• Rule — Word Choice/Collocation: Words like "built", "fabricated", and "manufactured" are associated with the physical/mechanical construction of objects, not with the creative development of fictional characters.

• "Produced" is the standard usage when referring to creative or media output (e.g., "the industry has produced many stars"), matching the tone of the passage about comics and their characters.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "built" is incorrect — "built" is typically used for physical structures (buildings, machines), not fictional characters.

• Option 3: "fabricated" is incorrect — "fabricated" carries a negative connotation of inventing false information/lies, which does not fit the neutral, factual tone of the passage.

• Option 4: "manufactured" is incorrect — "manufactured" refers to industrial, mechanical production of goods, which is inappropriate for describing the creation of comic characters.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check the connotation (positive/negative) and register (formal/informal, literal/figurative) of each option before selecting, not just its literal dictionary meaning.

• "Produced" is commonly used in the context of creative/media works: films, books, comics, art.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. created.

• Rule — Word Choice: "Created" specifically means to bring something new into existence, which is the exact sense required when talking about a character's first appearance/origin.

• The other options, while related in meaning, do not fit as precisely: "generated" is used more for processes/output (e.g., generating electricity, revenue), while "promoted"/"inspired" describe actions related to an already-existing character, not its origin.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 3: "promoted" is incorrect — "promoted" refers to publicizing or advancing something that already exists, not to its original creation.

NOTE

• "Create" is the standard verb for the origin of characters, stories, or works of art (e.g., "Sherlock Holmes was created by Arthur Conan Doyle").

Indrajal comics was set up in 1964 and (3) __________ Aabid Surti, who gave birth to a character called Bhadur in 1976 wearing kurta and jeans. Raj comics too (4) _________ into this sphere with their (5) _________ toons Nagraj, Tiranga and Shakti together called Brahman Rakshak (protectors of the universe).

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. employed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the relationship between "Indrajal comics" (an organisation) and Aabid Surti (a person who later created a character for them). The most appropriate word is "employed", meaning to give someone a paid job or to hire someone to do work.

• Rule — Word Choice: "Employed" is the standard verb used when an organisation hires or engages a person for creative/professional work, fitting the context of a comics company engaging a writer/artist.

• This fits logically: "Indrajal comics was set up in 1964 and employed Aabid Surti, who gave birth to a character called Bhadur in 1976" — the company hired him, and later he created the character.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "ordered" is incorrect — "ordered" means to command or to place a purchase order for goods, which does not fit the sense of hiring a person.

• Option 3: "contracted" is incorrect — while "contracted" can mean hiring someone for a specific task, it is more typically used for engaging firms/agencies for defined projects rather than describing an ongoing employment relationship, making "employed" the more natural and precise fit here.

• Option 4: "authorised" is incorrect — "authorised" means to give official permission for something, which does not fit the context of hiring a person to work.

NOTE

• "Employ" (to hire) should not be confused with "employ" (to use/utilize), which is a separate common meaning of the same word.

• Related words: employee, employer, employment, unemployed.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. entered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes Raj comics joining the field of superhero comics, following the pattern already set by Indrajal comics. The neutral, appropriate verb for a business/organisation joining a field or market is "entered" (commonly used with "into").

• Rule — Word Choice: "Entered into" is the standard, neutral collocation used to describe an organisation starting to operate in a particular field or sphere, e.g., "the company entered into the automobile sector."

• The other options ("invaded", "penetrated", "pierced") carry connotations of force, aggression, or forceful physical action, which do not suit the calm, factual tone of the passage describing a comics company's expansion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "invaded" is incorrect — "invaded" implies a forceful, often military or hostile, incursion, which is inappropriate for describing a business entering a creative field.

• Option 2: "penetrated" is incorrect — "penetrated" suggests forcing a way into something difficult to access, too strong/forceful a term for this neutral business context.

• Option 4: "pierced" is incorrect — "pierced" literally means to make a hole through something with a sharp object; it is entirely inappropriate in this figurative business context.

NOTE

• "Enter into" is the standard neutral collocation for businesses/organisations starting new ventures or fields (e.g., "enter into a partnership", "enter into the market").

• Words like "invade", "penetrate", "pierce" belong to a group connoting force or aggression and are usually inappropriate in neutral, factual business/informative contexts.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. famous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the characters Nagraj, Tiranga and Shakti, referred to collectively as Brahman Rakshak. The most fitting adjective to describe well-known comic characters is "famous", meaning known about by many people.

• Rule — Word Choice: The word chosen must naturally collocate with "toons" (cartoon characters) in a way that conveys their popularity/recognition, which "famous" does clearly and directly.

• Given that these are well-known, widely recognised Raj Comics characters, "famous" is the most natural and commonly used descriptor.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "noted" is incorrect — "noted" means well known for a particular quality or skill, and is typically used with "for" (e.g., "noted for his honesty"); it does not fit as naturally here as "famous".

• Option 2: "influential" is incorrect — "influential" means having great influence or impact on outcomes or decisions, a different quality from simply being well-known/popular.

• Option 4: "good" is incorrect — "good" is too generic and vague; it does not specifically convey the sense of wide recognition that the passage intends.

NOTE

• "Famous" collocates naturally with words describing people, characters, or things known widely (famous actor, famous landmark, famous toons/characters).

• Do not confuse "famous" (well known, usually positively) with "infamous" (well known for something bad).
